:::{#exm-convex-hessian}
#### Using the Hessian to show convexity

- For a symmetric positive semidefinite $\matr{A}$, $f(\vx) = \qform{\matr{A}}{\vx}$
  has [Hessian](vector-calculus.qmd#def-hessian) $2 \matr{A}$ (by the [Hessian of a quadratic form](vector-calculus.qmd#thm-hessian-quadratic)),
  which is positive semidefinite because $\tp{\vecf{h}} (2 \matr{A}) \vecf{h} = 2\,\tp{\vecf{h}} \matr{A} \vecf{h} \ge 0$;
  so $f$ is convex.
- $f(\vx) = x_1^2 + x_2^2 - 2 x_1$ has Hessian $2 \matr{I}_2$ (@exm-second-order-condition),
  which is positive definite, so $f$ is strictly convex.
- $f(\vx) = e^{2x_1 + x_2} - x_1$ has Hessian $e^{u} \sbmat{ 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 }$ with $u = 2x_1 + x_2$ (the [Hessian example](vector-calculus.qmd#exm-hessian)), and

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  \tp{\vecf{h}}\,\matr{H}_f(\vx)\,\vecf{h}
  &= e^{u} (4 h_1^2 + 4 h_1 h_2 + h_2^2) \\
  &= e^{u} (2 h_1 + h_2)^2 \\
  &\ge 0,
  \end{aligned}
  $$

  so $f$ is convex.
  The Hessian is not positive definite ($\vecf{h} = \tp{(1, -2)}$ gives $0$),
  so part 2 does not apply,
  and in fact $f$ is not strictly convex:
  along $\vx = t\,\tp{(1, -2)}$,

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  u &= 2t - 2t \\
  &= 0
  \end{aligned}
  $$

  and $f = 1 - t$ is linear in $t$,
  so the convexity inequality holds with equality there.

:::
